content:
You may be weighing a room you can rent by the day against a lease that needs construction before anyone can gather. Both can be real options where you live. This planting method still starts from a portable church. Compare a build-out before launch. Do not treat it as the path you already chose.

Use one sheet for both options. Write the costs, the first date you may actually gather, the volunteer load, and the approvals still open. A finished sheet does not sign a lease or start work. Everyfield does not score buildings, and it does not certify that a church should take on construction.

---

## Keep portable rent on the sheet

The Facilities Leader finds Sunday space, stays in contact with the owner, runs weekly setup and teardown, and watches for a later facilities plan. Looking ahead is not the same as renovating before Launch Sunday.

Portable rent means you use someone else's finished rooms on dates the owner has approved. You bring equipment in, and you take it out. Storage, transport, and a setup crew belong on the cost sheet. This method plans equipment for a rented facility and a weekly setup. You may adapt the plan locally. That does not make a pre-launch build-out the normal route.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"For which one of you, when he wants to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost to see if he has enough to complete it?"* — Luke 14:28 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## A lease can still need construction

Rent and a build-out are not opposites. You can lease a dedicated room and still have to change it before worship use.

A build-out, here, means work the landlord requires, or work you propose, before the church can gather. A banner you take home is not that work. Moving walls, adding rooms, changing exits, or changing the legal use of the building can be. Buying land and putting up a new building is a larger step. Send that to a separate review with your sending leaders and qualified advisers.

Conway School District in Washington prohibits alterations without prior approval. Its facility use agreement, updated January 5, 2021, names hanging signs and masking tape on walls and floors as examples. Users must return the facility to its original condition right after the event. That is one owner's rule. Ask yours, in writing, what the proposed agreement allows.

<Callout type="warning">
A spoken "that should be fine" is not approval. Ask a local attorney to read the lease or use agreement before you commit money or start work. Everyfield does not review contracts or decide whether a build-out is wise.
</Callout>

---

## Use the same questions for both options

Put this comparison beside your [venue comparison](/wiki/launch-team/comparing-and-scoring-venues), not in place of it. Keep a place out of the final choice while an essential permission is still open. Do not fold a missing answer into an average score.

### First date you may gather

| Portable rent | Leased build-out |
| --- | --- |
| First date the owner has approved in writing | Later of that date and the date local officials allow occupancy after the work |

### Written costs

| Portable rent | Leased build-out |
| --- | --- |
| Fees, deposits, staff, storage, transport, portable equipment, and insurance | Those costs, plus design, permits, construction, and work you may have to undo |

### Volunteer load

| Portable rent | Leased build-out |
| --- | --- |
| Weekly setup, room care, and teardown | Project oversight, plus setup if you still share or reset the room |

### Still unresolved

| Portable rent | Leased build-out |
| --- | --- |
| Use permission, insurance, and occupancy for your layout | Those items, plus consent to alter, permits, and any change-of-use approval |

Conway charges for staff on site to open and lock doors, run lights and heat, set chairs, and do routine cleanup. Applicants handle special setup and cleanup unless they asked for that help on the form. Ask which tasks volunteers must do and which tasks you must pay the owner to do.

One figure does not choose the building. In this method, 50 to 100 adults is a benchmark, not a sign that every church is ready to build. Money on hand is a different question from whether people are giving.

<Callout type="insight">
A large gift can make a build-out look settled. It is not. Ask whether people are giving, and ask separately whether the church can carry the written costs if that gift is late, restricted, or already spent.
</Callout>

---

## Itemize costs from the papers in front of you

There is no Everyfield price for rent or construction. Do not copy another city's fee sheet into your budget.

Conway's rental cost sheet, checked October 26, 2026, separates room or field charges from custodian time, kitchen use, stage equipment, and a deposit. It requires a nonrefundable deposit of 25 percent of the rental fee two weeks before the event. Treat those lines as questions, not as your rates. Confirm the current sheet with the district if you apply there.

For a leased build-out, ask the owner and a design professional to price design, permits, construction, inspections, fixtures you may not keep, insurance during the work, and rent for months you still cannot gather. Tie each figure to the quote or letter it came from. If a cell says "about," mark it unresolved.

Your [first-year budget](/wiki/administrative/financial/first-year-budget-planning) already has lines for worship rent, storage, and portable equipment. Add build-out lines only from written quotes. A coach, if you have one, can help you read the sheet. Everyfield does not do that work in the app, and this article is not financial advice.

---

## Separate a finish date from a use date

A proposal can name a day the crew hopes to finish. You cannot gather on that hope. The gathering date follows the date you may legally occupy the rooms.

In New York City, a certificate of occupancy states a legal use. An existing building needs a current or amended certificate when use, egress, or occupancy type changes. No one may legally occupy the building until the Department of Buildings issues a certificate of occupancy or a temporary one. Most construction there needs a permit. Some minor work does not. Those are New York City rules, checked October 26, 2026.

Building codes in the United States mostly belong to state and local governments. The National Institute of Standards and Technology notes that most jurisdictions start from a model code and may tighten or loosen it. Ask your building department and fire marshal which rooms, layout, and use their approval covers. Conway requires events to meet Skagit County and Washington occupancy and fire rules. Your county will name its own.

<Callout type="important">
The local examples and the federal rule below were checked October 26, 2026. Confirm current fees, permit rules, occupancy, and insurance with the owner and the agencies that govern your building before you rely on them.
</Callout>

If that use date slips past Launch Sunday, write the fallback before you sign. Name the portable room you can still reserve, what it costs, and who can move the launch date. Do not wait for the week an inspector says no.

---

## A federal exemption is not a local permit

The Department of Justice Title III rule does not apply to a religious entity. Its manual says the exemption covers all of that entity's activities, religious or secular, including activities that would otherwise look like a public accommodation.

The exemption does not answer local permit rules, fire rules, or the landlord's approval of alterations. Ask the attorney and the building department. Do not treat the exemption as a permit.

---

## Write down how you would leave

Portable rent ends when the reserved dates end, or sooner if the owner revokes permission. Conway may refuse or revoke use of a school building or grounds. If rental has been paid, the form says the district refunds that rental less its expense. A user who cancels needs at least 24 hours' notice, or the user bears the related costs. Your owner may be stricter. Ask, and keep the answer with the agreement. Take other contract questions to the [rental agreement review](/wiki/launch-team/facility-rental-agreements).

A build-out can keep costing money after you stop gathering. Before this comparison can support a commitment, ask a local attorney what the lease says about who owns the improvements, whether you must restore the space, what you owe if you leave early, whether a late project lets either side walk away, and what happens to the deposit and to rent in a month you cannot occupy.

- [ ] Costs for both options are written and tied to a document.
- [ ] The first lawful use date is separate from a hoped-for finish date.
- [ ] Volunteer tasks and paid owner tasks are named.
- [ ] Open approvals stay unresolved, not averaged into a score.
- [ ] A portable fallback is named if the work runs late.
- [ ] A local attorney has reviewed how you would leave.
- [ ] The Facilities Leader, treasurer, and Senior Pastor have read the sheet.

---

## Leave the decision with the people who will carry it

Bring the sheet to your sending leaders as well. If a build-out still has open approvals, keep planning the portable route. That remains this method's working assumption until your leaders and qualified advisers say otherwise, in writing.

A score can organize the talk. It cannot permit an alteration, and it cannot tell you the church is spiritually ready. Those judgments stay with people, not with software.

claim_check.notes: Owner review by Sebastian; no model review per his 2026-10-26 instruction.

rulings: Bryan ruled B16 = Option B: "Compare both before launch" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).

Wording: kept the backlog title Choosing Rent or Build-Out and slug launch-team/choosing-rent-or-build-out. sort_order 3 sits after Comparing and Scoring Venues (1) and Planning Services Around Room Capacity (2), and before Facility Rental Agreements (10).

Wording: buying land or constructing a new building is outside this comparison. Option B covers portable rental and leased space that needs a build-out. A ground-up project goes to a separate review with sending leaders and qualified advisers.

Wording: no national dollar table and no named church real-estate vendor. Written costs come from the owner's documents and local professionals, so the article gives cost categories without financial advice or a provider endorsement.

Wording: the Title III religious-entity exemption is named so readers do not assume that federal public-accommodation rule decides the project. It is not treated as permission to skip local permits, fire rules, or the landlord's approval.
Wording: portable rent stays this method's working assumption until leaders and qualified advisers decide otherwise in writing. A build-out is compared, not presented as the default.
